samples.summary: `saved-locally` is excluded from `mayHaveUnsent`, so the in-app navigation guard is dropped — but leaving a document detaches it, and the SDK's detach deletes the on-disk entry without archiving it
samples.evidence: `const mayHaveUnsent = stranded || state === 'saving';` (line 114) with `stranded = state === 'not-saved'` (line 78). The new `saved-locally` state therefore registers neither the `beforeunload` handler (line 125) nor `useNavigationGuard` (line 155), nor the probe (`use-unsaved-work-probe.ts:24`). For a *reload* that is correct: the entry survives and resumes. For an **in-app route change** it is not: this diff's own documentation states that `detachDocument` calls `removeFromStore` unconditionally on its success path (`packages/frontend/src/lib/wafflebase-doc-store.ts:764-771`), and `WafflebaseDocStore.remove()` archives only when `expectLoss` was latched — which happens exclusively from the `local-changes-dropped` handler (`durable-yorkie-provider.tsx` `DurableLossWatch`), never on an ordinary detach. `saved-locally` is reachable while `connected` is true (`sync-state.ts` returns it for `connected && syncFailed && durable`), where the detach RPC can succeed even though pushes are being rejected. Result: one click on a sidebar link unmounts the provider, the detach removes the only durable copy, the in-memory queue goes with it, and nothing warned the user — the exact loss the guard existed to prevent, now suppressed by the state that promises safety.

samples.summary: `held.current` is mutated during render alongside a render-phase `setState`; a render React discards leaves the latched clientKey/durable decision committed
samples.evidence: Lines 269-282 mutate the ref (`held.current = { subject, durable, clientKey }`) and conditionally call `setStoodDown(null)` inside the render body. Ref mutation during render is not rolled back when React throws a render away (concurrent rendering / Suspense retry), so a latch written from a render whose `durable`/`clientKey` values never committed can survive as the decision the next committed render reads at line 283-286. Because that latch is precisely what decides whether a stable `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}` client is mounted, a stale-but-latched `durable: true` publishes a client key for an election this tab may not hold — the two-tabs-one-actor case `durable-session.ts` exists to prevent, whose cost is silent edit loss.

samples.summary: `deleteDocuments` dereferences the parsed body without a null guard, turning an empty/`null` JSON response into a TypeError
samples.evidence: `const result = (await response.json()) as { deleted: string[] };` then `result.deleted ?? []`. `response.json()` resolves to `null` for a body of literal `null`, and `result.deleted` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`. The previous code (`return response.json()`) propagated `null` to the caller instead. The cast hides it from any type checker, and the frontend package has no `tsc` lane at all.

samples.summary: The lapse fallback reports `"another-tab"` for every non-durable reason it does not enumerate, including "no signed-in identity"
samples.evidence: Lines 291-299: after `unsupported`/`not-permitted`/`not-enabled`, anything else falls through to `"another-tab"`. But `decided.durable` is also false when `person` is undefined (line 351 requires `!person`), when the election is simply undecided, and for the `pdf-` structural exclusion. The chip then renders "This document is open in another tab, and that tab is the one saving it to this device." (`sync-status-tooltip.ts` LAPSE_REASONS) — a concretely false statement the design requires to be accurate ("Its tooltip must name which case applies"), sending the user to close a tab that does not exist.

samples.summary: A write refused because the preference was switched off is reported through `onWriteFailure`, which latches `writesFailing` permanently and mislabels the lapse as `write-failed`
samples.evidence: `refuseIfDisabled` (around line 400-412) calls `this.reportWriteFailure(err)` before throwing. In `durable-yorkie-provider.tsx` that handler does `setWritesFailing(true)`, which is documented as latched and never reset. So (a) the tooltip says "This device could not be written to." when the true cause is `not-enabled`, and (b) if the user switches the preference off and back on with the document still open — the client is deliberately left mounted — the store resumes accepting writes while the chip is stuck reporting the document non-durable for the rest of the open. The latch outlives its cause.

samples.summary: `store.close()` runs in the unmount cleanup while the async housekeeping chain and the recovery toast's click handler still hold the same store, silently reopening an un-closed connection
samples.evidence: The cleanup (lines 200-209) sets `cancelled = true` and calls `store.close()`, but the in-flight IIFE can be parked on `fetchDocuments()`/`fetchDocument()` and `offerRecoverableWork(store, ...)` still uses it; more importantly the `Save a copy` handler installed at line 287 captures `store` and survives the unmount because the toast is `duration: Infinity` and `<Toaster />` lives outside the router. `WafflebaseDocStore.open()` clears `opening`/`db` on close and lazily reopens, so those calls transparently open a second IndexedDB connection that nothing ever closes — which is exactly the state that blocks another tab's `deleteDatabase`/version change.

samples.summary: Releasing and immediately re-requesting the same election name can be refused, because the Web Lock is only freed once the parked promise settles a turn later
samples.evidence: `release()` (end of `acquireDurableSession`) deletes the map entry and calls `releaseLock()`, which resolves the promise the `webLocks()` callback is parked on; the browser frees the name only when that promise settles. The suite acknowledges this by inserting `flush()` before re-acquiring (`durable-session.test.ts`, "lets a later tab in once the name is free"). A remount of the same `docKey` in the same task (a React key change, or an unmount/mount pair outside StrictMode's shared-election window) therefore re-requests with `ifAvailable: true` while the name is still held, gets `undefined`, and the document stays non-durable for the rest of that open with nothing retrying — the effect's dependencies have not changed.

finding.summary: `saved-locally` is excluded from `mayHaveUnsent`, so the in-app navigation guard is dropped — but leaving a document detaches it, and the SDK's detach deletes the on-disk entry without archiving it
finding.evidence: `const mayHaveUnsent = stranded || state === 'saving';` (line 114) with `stranded = state === 'not-saved'` (line 78). The new `saved-locally` state therefore registers neither the `beforeunload` handler (line 125) nor `useNavigationGuard` (line 155), nor the probe (`use-unsaved-work-probe.ts:24`). For a *reload* that is correct: the entry survives and resumes. For an **in-app route change** it is not: this diff's own documentation states that `detachDocument` calls `removeFromStore` unconditionally on its success path (`packages/frontend/src/lib/wafflebase-doc-store.ts:764-771`), and `WafflebaseDocStore.remove()` archives only when `expectLoss` was latched — which happens exclusively from the `local-changes-dropped` handler (`durable-yorkie-provider.tsx` `DurableLossWatch`), never on an ordinary detach. `saved-locally` is reachable while `connected` is true (`sync-state.ts` returns it for `connected && syncFailed && durable`), where the detach RPC can succeed even though pushes are being rejected. Result: one click on a sidebar link unmounts the provider, the detach removes the only durable copy, the in-memory queue goes with it, and nothing warned the user — the exact loss the guard existed to prevent, now suppressed by the state that promises safety.

verdict.reason: All cited code is present exactly as described. sync-status-chip.tsx:78 defines `stranded = state === 'not-saved'` and :114 defines `mayHaveUnsent = stranded || state === 'saving'`, which excludes the new `saved-locally` state; both the `beforeunload` registration (:124-135) and `useNavigationGuard` (:155-171) are gated on that flag, and use-unsaved-work-probe.ts:24 repeats the same exclusion. sync-state.ts:75-85 confirms `saved-locally` is returned whenever pending work is durable, including `connected && syncFailed`. Grep shows `useNavigationGuard` has exactly one production call site (sync-status-chip.tsx:155) and `registerUnsavedWorkProbe` only use-unsaved-work-probe.ts:28 plus the unrelated upload queue, so no guard elsewhere covers a durable document left by an in-app route change. On the deletion side, wafflebase-doc-store.ts:795-852 archives only when `expectedLosses` holds the key (809/829) and otherwise deletes snapshot, header and change log outright (847-849); the only product caller of `expectLoss` is the `local-changes-dropped` subscription in durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:308-313 (plus the unreportable fallback at 325), never an ordinary detach. The repo's own comments (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:764-771) and design doc (docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md:266-272) assert that `detachDocument` calls `removeFromStore` unconditionally on its success path, i.e. unmounting deletes the durable entry without archiving. The single unverifiable link is SDK detach semantics (no vendored SDK sources), and the design is self-contradictory there (sync-status.md:487-491 says the unmount pushes a final pack, while :274-277 says the unmount discards the queue with nothing said — the stated reason the guard exists). That residual uncertainty cannot support any named refutation ground, so the finding stands.

finding.summary: `held.current` is mutated during render alongside a render-phase `setState`; a render React discards leaves the latched clientKey/durable decision committed
finding.evidence: Lines 269-282 mutate the ref (`held.current = { subject, durable, clientKey }`) and conditionally call `setStoodDown(null)` inside the render body. Ref mutation during render is not rolled back when React throws a render away (concurrent rendering / Suspense retry), so a latch written from a render whose `durable`/`clientKey` values never committed can survive as the decision the next committed render reads at line 283-286. Because that latch is precisely what decides whether a stable `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}` client is mounted, a stale-but-latched `durable: true` publishes a client key for an election this tab may not hold — the two-tabs-one-actor case `durable-session.ts` exists to prevent, whose cost is silent edit loss.

verdict.reason: The quoted code exists (collab-document-provider.tsx:269-282 mutates `held.current` during render and calls `setStoodDown(null)` in the render body), but the claimed harm — a latched `durable: true`/`clientKey` from a discarded render mounting a stable client for an election this tab does not hold — is unreachable, guarded at four points. (1) The latch only writes when `ready = settled && identified` (line 268), and `settled` requires `answered` (use-durable-document.ts:232,254), so no latch occurs before the election has answered. (2) `durable = answered && !!decision?.session` (use-durable-document.ts:233) and `session` is only ever set from a resolved `acquireDurableSession` handle (use-durable-document.ts:205-215), which resolves a handle only on an actually granted Web Lock (durable-session.ts:437-464); React discards render *work*, it does not roll back the `setDecision` update, so any render observing `durable: true` — committed or not — corresponds to a lock genuinely held. (3) `subject`, `durable` and `clientKey` are all derived in the same render from the same `person?.id`/`docKey` (collab-document-provider.tsx:256, use-durable-document.ts:249), and the tuple is consumed only when `held.current?.subject === subject` (283-286), so a surviving latch always belongs to the subject it is read under and cannot pair one person's key with another's subject. (4) The only demotion under a live latch is `standDown`, whose sole caller `giveUp` (263-266) sets `stoodDown = subject`, which line 284 excludes; the effect-cleanup release (use-durable-document.ts:217-220) fires only when `eligible`/`userId`/`docKey` change, and `eligible` is latched per identity (166-171) while a `userId`/`docKey` change also moves the component `subject` (256) and forces a re-latch. The inverse direction (latching `false` where `true` would commit) is also impossible because `decision` is written once per hook subject (192-221). What remains is a render-purity style concern with no demonstrable wrong behavior, which is not blocking under the Correctness rubric.

finding.summary: The session-start reconcile destroys the archive of every document that was deleted upstream — the exact unsent work the recovery offer exists to hand back — before the offer is ever made.
finding.evidence: `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments()` enumerates `storedDocumentIds({ archives: true })` and, for every id not in the server listing, calls `purgeDocument(id, { archives: "drop", skipOpen: true, updatedSince: listedAt })` (offline-erase.ts:487-497). "The document was deleted or GC'd upstream" is one of the three documented causes of an archive (offline-copy.ts header), and `GET /documents` hard-deletes (`document.service.ts:126 prisma.document.delete`), so such an id can never be in `accessible`. `dropArchivesForDocument` only spares rows with `archivedAt >= updatedSince` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1031-1036) — an archive written in a *previous* session always fails that — or rows whose document is open, which a deleted document never is. And `OfflineRuntime` runs the reconcile strictly *before* `offerRecoverableWork` (offline-runtime.tsx:157 then 192), and offers only once per mount, so an archive created mid-session is first offered next session, by which time the reconcile has already deleted it. This directly contradicts the deliberate exemption on the same path: `purgeOfflineDocuments` defaults to `archives: "keep"` precisely because "'deleted upstream' is one of the three paths that produce an archive" (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:886-889). Net effect: the only durable copy of work the server never took is silently deleted, which is the loss the feature exists to prevent.

verdict.reason: Verified in repo: purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments (offline-erase.ts:487-497) drops archives (`archives: "drop"`) for every stored id absent from the server listing. Deleted-upstream documents can never appear in that listing (hard delete at document.service.ts:129; listing fetched at offline-runtime.tsx:155), and dropArchivesForDocument's two exemptions (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1031-1037) spare only archives with archivedAt >= listedAt or whose docKey is currently live — neither holds for an archive written in a previous session for a document nobody has open. OfflineRuntime runs the reconcile (offline-runtime.tsx:157) strictly before offerRecoverableWork (offline-runtime.tsx:192), once per mount, so a mid-session archive is first offerable next session, after that session's reconcile has deleted it. This makes the explicit deleted-upstream recovery arm (offline-runtime.tsx:264-278, 404 fallback) unreachable across sessions and contradicts the stated default at wafflebase-doc-store.ts:885-889 and offline-erase.ts:385-389. Net effect is silent loss of the only durable copy of unsent work — data loss on a real path, hence critical and in the correctness lane. No guard or caller elsewhere prevents it: the other purge path (offline-erase.ts:404-406) keeps archives but cannot stop the reconcile.

finding.summary: On the currently pinned build the chip tells every user with unsent work "This browser cannot save documents locally" — a build-time library check reported as a browser capability.
finding.evidence: `lapse` is computed as `!supportsClientKey() ? "unsupported" : ...` (collab-document-provider.tsx:291-299), and `supportsClientKey()` reads `__YORKIE_REACT_VERSION__` against `MinClientKeyVersion = "0.7.23"` (yorkie-capabilities.ts). `packages/frontend/package.json:66` pins `@yorkie-js/react` at `0.7.22`, so the predicate is false on every build shipped by this PR. The scope wraps both branches and the editor subtree, and `SyncStatusChip` renders inside it (document-detail.tsx:910-921 → SiteHeader → SyncStatusChip), so `tooltipFor(...)` appends `LAPSE_REASONS.unsupported` = "This browser cannot save documents locally." to the `not-saved` tooltip for *every* user who goes offline today — including on the share route, where the correct reason is `not-permitted`. The statement is false (it is the app build, not the browser) and it is on the commonest path the chip has.

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding is present and reachable. collab-document-provider.tsx:291-299 orders `!supportsClientKey()` ahead of `!permitted`/`!offlineEnabled`; yorkie-capabilities.ts:24,76-82 resolves that predicate from the build-time pin, vite.config.ts:414-418 injects it from package.json:66 which pins @yorkie-js/react at 0.7.22 (< MinClientKeyVersion 0.7.23), so `lapse === "unsupported"` for every non-durable document on every build this PR ships. The scope wraps both branches at collab-document-provider.tsx:349-350 and DurabilityLapseScope only inherits when the inner value is undefined (durable-document-context.ts:140-153); DurableYorkieProvider — the only deeper publisher — cannot mount on this build. SyncStatusChip reads the lapse (sync-status-chip.tsx:79) and passes it to tooltipFor (:322), which appends LAPSE_REASONS.unsupported = 'This browser cannot save documents locally.' in the `not-saved` case (sync-status-tooltip.ts:30,111-112). That chip is mounted for owned documents via document-detail.tsx:910-921 -> SiteHeader syncStatus (:685-717). So every user who goes offline with unsent work is told a build-time library limitation is a browser capability. On the share route, shared-document.tsx:1017's NonDurableScope only sets permitted=false (use-durable-document.ts:61-81), so the `unsupported` branch short-circuits the intentionally-suppressed `not-permitted` reason and substitutes the same false sentence. No guard suppresses the string: sync-status-chip.tsx:95-99 gates only the offer, not the tooltip reason. This is a mis-ordered condition yielding a wrong user-visible result on the commonest path the feature exists to describe — in the correctness lane, not refutable on not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope grounds.
